title: How Monopoly Works
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore the history of Monopoly, starting with Mr. Monopoly's nickname and the Monopoly Companion's character names, then Henry George's Georgism and Lizzie Magie's 1904-era Landlord's Game with its two rule sets. They trace the game through Ruth Hoskins, the Quaker Jessie and Eugene Raiford, and Charles Darrow, whom Parker Brothers bought the game from, and explain how Lizzie's patent was bought. They discuss Monopoly's Atlantic City board, the evolution of tokens, the board layout and cards, house rules, auctions, mortgages, jail, and strategy (utilities, orange properties, three-house rule). They cover Ralph Anspach's anti-Monopoly game, Parker Brothers' lawsuit, and his Supreme Court win. The episode ends with a rapid-fire Facebook question segment on unrelated topics such as vacuums, pets, favorite books, and movie stars.

segments.title: Opening banter and Mr. Monopoly
segments.summary: Hosts joke about Mr. Monopoly's monocle and his full name Rich Uncle Pennybags (Millburn Pennybags), note the Monopoly Companion book, and remark that Monopoly has more supplemental history than typical topics.

segments.title: Georgism and The Landlord's Game
segments.summary: Origins of Monopoly in folk games influenced by Henry George's Georgism, which proposed taxing land value. Lizzie Magie created The Landlord's Game with two rule sets, one rewarding wealth accumulation and one rewarding the community, and patented it.

segments.title: Quaker players and Ruth Hoskins
segments.summary: Lizzie's game spread among socialist-leaning East Coast circles. Quaker players introduced fixed prices instead of auctions and tokens. Ruth Hoskins and Jessie and Eugene Raiford changed rules toward the modern Monopoly, and the game passed to Todd and then Charles Darrow.

segments.title: Charles Darrow and the sale to Parker Brothers
segments.summary: Charles Darrow, a radiator salesman during the Depression, sold a copied version of the game to Parker Brothers, which first rejected it. Darrow sold it at Wanamaker's in Philadelphia, and Parker Brothers later bought the idea and Lizzie Magie's patent, along with some of her other games.

segments.title: Monopoly's Atlantic City board and Mary Pilon's article
segments.summary: The board's Atlantic City properties reflect the city's geography and neighborhoods. Hosts mention the Reading Railroad, New York Avenue's gay scene, and the misspelled Marvin Gardens.

segments.title: Monopoly versions, tokens and board contents
segments.summary: Hundreds of licensed Monopoly versions exist, including corporate and Star Wars editions. Official tokens changed over time: the iron was replaced by a cat in 2013 after fan voting, and the cannon and battleship were retired. The set includes houses, hotels, cards, title deeds and play money.

segments.title: Board layout, squares, cards and setup
segments.summary: The board has 40 squares plus the split jail, including properties, railroads, utilities, tax squares, Go (salary of two hundred dollars), Chance and Community Chest. Setup covers starting cash distribution and the goal of bankrupting opponents. Hosts discuss two-player games.

segments.title: Auctions, monopolies, houses and mortgages
segments.summary: Declined properties go to auction, with the banker and the decliner able to bid. A full color group is a monopoly that doubles rent, allowing houses and hotels. Mortgaging a property with improvements requires selling the buildings back first, and redeeming the mortgage costs the amount plus ten percent.

segments.title: Jail rules and Monopoly strategy
segments.summary: Ways to go to jail and get out, including doubles, the fifty-dollar payment, and the Get Out of Jail Free card. Strategy covers buying everything, avoiding hoarding cash, the three-house limit, the weak utilities and Boardwalk/Park Place, and the orange properties landed on most often. Hosts also mention a Monopoly World Championship and a Scientific American probability article.

segments.title: Ralph Anspach, anti-Monopoly and the lawsuit
segments.summary: Economics professor Ralph Anspach made anti-Monopoly to explain monopolies to his son. Parker Brothers sued and obtained his stock. Anspach fought the case, found evidence that Darrow did not invent the game, and won at the Supreme Court. His book and the later Anti-Monopoly edition are mentioned.

segments.title: Listener questions and sign-off
segments.summary: Rapid-fire Facebook questions on vacuums, marriage, pets, favorite books, and movie stars, followed by sign-off and website reminders.
